[Step 02] Set a specific first goal. Aim to play one simple, 30–60-second song or accompaniment at a steady pace within four weeks. Schedule 15–20 minutes of practice on five days each week.

[Step 03] Get the essentials ready. Obtain a playable instrument, a metronome app, and a phone for recording yourself. Get a tuner if your instrument requires tuning, plus any necessary accessories, such as a pick or drumsticks.

[Step 04] Learn how to set up and handle the instrument. Follow a beginner demonstration covering posture, hand position, setup, and basic care. Tune when needed, keep your movements relaxed, and stop if playing causes pain.

[Step 05] Learn terminology through physical examples. Start with *beat*—the steady pulse; *tempo*—its speed; *rhythm*—the timing pattern; and *melody*—a sequence of pitches. Learn instrument-specific terms by locating the relevant parts, such as keys, strings, or frets.

[Step 06] Choose a learning method that does not require sheet music. Use close-up video demonstrations and recordings. Depending on your instrument, supplement these with chord diagrams, guitar tablature, labeled keys, or spoken rhythm patterns. Choose one structured beginner course so each lesson builds on the previous one.

[Step 07] Practice keeping a steady beat. Set a metronome to about 60 beats per minute. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” repeatedly and clap once per click for one minute. Then play one comfortable note or drum sound with each click.

[Step 08] Build a small set of basic movements. For a melody instrument, learn three to five comfortable notes; for chord accompaniment, learn two easy chords; for percussion, learn one basic groove. Practice producing clear sounds slowly before increasing speed.

[Step 09] Choose a suitable first song. Find a beginner arrangement using mostly the notes, chords, or groove you already know. Listen several times, then hum the melody or tap its rhythm. Start with one verse, chorus, or short section.

[Step 10] Learn the song in short phrases. Listen to or watch two to five seconds, pause, and copy it. Use slow playback that preserves pitch when available. Repeat until you can reproduce the phrase correctly three times, then learn the next phrase.

[Step 11] Practice difficult transitions separately. Isolate the two notes, chords, or movements around each hesitation. Repeat that transition slowly, then reconnect it to the surrounding phrase. Increase the metronome by about five beats per minute only when the movement stays accurate and relaxed.

[Step 12] Join the phrases and record a complete attempt. Begin at a comfortable tempo and try to maintain the beat through small mistakes. Listen back for one priority—such as uneven timing, unclear notes, or pauses—and address that issue in your next practice.

[Step 13] Experiment with what you know. Make a short musical phrase using your familiar notes, chords, or percussion sounds. Change one feature at a time, such as rhythm or note order. For pitched instruments, also try humming a short phrase and finding it by ear.

[Step 14] Follow a repeatable daily routine. Spend two minutes setting up, three minutes on rhythm, four minutes on technique, eight minutes on your song, and three minutes playing freely or recording. On busy days, do five focused minutes on one difficult phrase.

[Step 15] Review progress weekly and adjust. Log your practice time, comfortable tempo, and next practice target. Compare recordings once a week, and seek feedback from a teacher or experienced player if a problem persists. Treat four weeks as a checkpoint: keep developing the same song if needed, or choose another that adds just one new skill."}
